extracted.intended_audience: students (grades 7-12), teachers, and parents preparing submissions to the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for students (and their teachers/parents) on eligibility, preparing, and submitting art and writing works to the Scholastic Art & Writing Awards, plus tips to increase chances of regional and national recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students in grades 7–12, age 13 years or older who reside in the United States, U.S. territories, U.S. Military bases, or Canada can enter; international students are also encouraged to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure you meet grade/age/residency requirements before submitting; check specific regional program rules if uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category selection (art & writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the category that best fits your piece from the provided art and writing categories (e.g., Photography, Short Story, Poetry, Design, Flash Fiction, etc.). Portfolios are a separate category for graduating seniors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may participate in one or two categories depending on interests. Pick the category that most closely matches the work’s form and intent to avoid misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission timeline and regional deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The awards open in September and deadlines vary by region (some regions as early as December 1; others in January).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check your specific state/region's deadline (regional dates provided). Plan and upload well before your region’s cutoff to avoid last-minute issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account creation and school linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an account in the awards portal; students and educators can link accounts to a school or educational program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking to a school/educational program joins you to the community and may be required by some regional programs. Start the account set-up early to resolve any access issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uploading work: high-quality digital representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Upload artwork as digital images and choose high-quality images that truly represent your inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select clear, well-lit, high-resolution images that convey the piece’s detail and intent. Seek feedback from teachers/family when choosing which images to submit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entry fees and fee waivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Entry fees are $10 for individual entries and $30 for portfolios; a fee waiver option is available if fees are a barrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for entry fees and apply for a fee waiver if needed. Confirm current fees on the official site as they may change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors look for works that break away from convention, blur boundaries between genres, and challenge notions of how a particular concept or emotion can be expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To stand out, create work from your own experience and imagination rather than imitating others. Avoid derivative work; make sure the piece expresses a unique perspective or approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skills (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should show practiced techniques and abilities to enhance and skillfully express a particular perspective or vision with clear intention and execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrable technical competence should serve the piece’s intent. Practice, refinement, and clear choices in execution strengthen a submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal voice or vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should communicate an authentic and unique point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges value authenticity — the work should convey a coherent personal sensibility or message rather than generic or impersonal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art: clear subject matter and intention
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear subject matter and intention of the piece: choosing a subject that can best express the intention behind your art piece is critical to give your work meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what you want to say with the work and select a subject that directly supports that intention; clarity of purpose helps judges read your piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art: techniques to communicate subject and intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques are the use of the principles of art to convey meaning — use of value, color, composition, line weights, light contours, proportion, foreground/background, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ appropriate compositional and technical choices (value contrast, color harmony, varied line weight, proportion accuracy) to reinforce your intended message and create dimension and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art: materials matched to technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials used in conjunction with technique: pick a medium you genuinely understand so you can best utilize different techniques to clearly express yourself (e.g., choose proper paper for gouache vs watercolor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select materials appropriate to your methods and master their use; poor material choices can hamper the intended effect (e.g., wrong paper for a medium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art: composition and proportion mastery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastering the rule of composition and proportion is essential, especially for human figures, faces, and postures; background and foreground need correct treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study composition rules and human anatomy/proportion if relevant; properly balancing foreground/background and accurate proportions improves believability and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing: research
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, do proper research to understand target audience and topic; research provides information and sources to back claims or give context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use credible sources where needed, ground nonfiction in evidence, and use research to enrich fiction’s realism and worldbuilding; document sources as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing: planning and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning is essential to maintain logical flow of ideas or events and stay true to overarching arguments or themes; a clear plan/outlines help avoid losing track of the main message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create outlines or story maps to ensure coherence. Make sure every scene/paragraph contributes to the central idea or narrative arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing: editing and revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing is crucial — from grammatical checks to fixing tone; the amount of effort in editing is visible to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively revise for clarity, grammar, pacing, and tone. Seek feedback and perform multiple edit passes; polished presentation signals seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic voice development practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing voice requires self-reflection, exploration, imitation-then-transformation, and learning from failure; voice evolves over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use journaling, vision boards, and reflective questions (e.g., What do you love? Who are your favorite artists/authors? What motivates you?) to discover consistent themes and motivations that inform your voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism avoidance and citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitted work must be different from what others have created and not be copied from original work; cite sources regardless of category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check for accidental plagiarism (use Turnitin or Grammarly for writing), and always cite sources when appropriate; plagiarized work is disqualified and unethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Scholastic resources and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alliance provides resources such as Art Portfolio Panel, Writing Portfolio Panel, and an Uploading Portfolios walkthrough; view past winners in the Scholastic Awards Gallery and Best Teen Writing and Art Work collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch the panel videos and walkthroughs for concrete advice on strong portfolios, and study past winning works to understand successful approaches and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymous, professional judging standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging is conducted anonymously by academic and arts professionals (including notable alumni), ensuring selection free from bias regarding the student’s gender, age, ethnicity, or hometown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because judging is anonymous, avoid including identifying info in the submission materials; focus on the work’s merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancement and award tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional awards include Gold Key, Silver Key, Honorable Mention, American Visions/Voices Nominee; Gold Key entries are considered for National Awards (Gold Medals, Silver Medals with Distinction, Silver Medals) and scholarships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the tiered system: regional recognition can lead to national consideration. Submitting to appropriate categories and meeting technical/originality/voice standards increases chances of advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition, publication, and scholarship outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Award-winning students may be featured in exhibitions and publications and are eligible for cash awards and academic scholarships (including tuition-based awards and scholarships up to $10,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation quality (images, writing polish) matters because winning work is often exhibited or published; think of submissions as both competitive entries and public-facing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom/workshop preparation model
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation involves working with literary and media texts, planning, writing, workshopping, re-shaping, and re-workshopping to refine skills in reading, writing, speaking, and listening; final portfolios act as a catalog of thoughtful work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative classroom/workshop processes to generate and refine portfolio pieces; teachers should encourage sourcing additional competitions/publications for further opportunities.
